   Say you invest $10,000 in a stock that pays no dividend. It returns 10% a year, and you sell it after 20 years. You’ll have made a capital gain of $57,275.

   If inflation averaged 3% during that span, though, then half of your profit can be traced to that increase in prices (the difference between compounding at 7% and 10%). Why, the argument goes, should people then be expected to pay taxes on that “phantom gain” from which they derived no real boost to their wealth?

   There have been occasional calls from Congress, most recently this year , to redefine capital gains so as to index them to prices. But what sounds reasonable and fair would create wild distortions.

   For example, how much more yield would people then demand for owning bonds when appreciating assets like stocks are shielded? And what would governments and companies then have to pay to borrow? Long-term interest rates are already near multidecade highs worldwide .

   Contributing to a tax-deferred account such as a 401(k), beyond snagging a company match, might no longer make sense either. Withdrawals are taxed like ordinary income, inflation included. Older Americans who’ve spent decades building nest eggs in those accounts would feel like chumps.

   So would lower-income people who have little in the way of retirement assets to begin with. Capital gains already get favorable tax treatment compared with wage income. The Tax Foundation estimated that the top fifth of taxpayers would receive a boost to after tax income more than 10 times as great as the lowest fifth if gains were indexed to prices.

   It’s unlikely to happen with so much red ink already flowing in Washington. The Yale Budget Lab calculated that indexing capital gains would cost Uncle Sam $1 trillion over a decade if applied retroactively. 

   Even so, the conversation over inflation’s drag is worth having. The bull market of the past several years may have left savers feeling rich, but it got a boost from gains that don’t translate into nearly as much bread, gasoline or college tuition. 

   The S&P 500’s annualized return over the past five calendar years falls from 14.3% to 9.5% when adjusted for buying power. Inflation ran above the Federal Reserve’s target for nearly that entire span. 

   The preceding 10 years looks less impressive at first glance with a headline annualized gain of just 13.8%. But investors kept much more of it with an inflation-adjusted return of 11.8%.

   Even before accounting for capital gains, “the cruelest tax” sneakily picks thrifty people’s pockets with no act of Congress required.

Phantom gains, real money

 

Inflation can be taxing—literally.

 

Say you invest $10,000 in a stock that pays no dividend. It returns 10% a year, and you sell it after 20 years. You’ll have made a capital gain of $57,275.

 

If inflation averaged 3% during that span, though, then half of your profit can be traced to that increase in prices (the difference between compounding at 7% and 10%). Why, the argument goes, should people then be expected to pay taxes on that “phantom gain” from which they derived no real boost to their wealth?

 

There have been occasional calls from Congress, most recently this year, to redefine capital gains so as to index them to prices. But what sounds reasonable and fair would create wild distortions.

 

For example, how much more yield would people then demand for owning bonds when appreciating assets like stocks are shielded? And what would governments and companies then have to pay to borrow? Long-term interest rates are already near multidecade highs worldwide.

 

Contributing to a tax-deferred account such as a 401(k), beyond snagging a company match, might no longer make sense either. Withdrawals are taxed like ordinary income, inflation included. Older Americans who’ve spent decades building nest eggs in those accounts would feel like chumps.

 

So would lower-income people who have little in the way of retirement assets to begin with. Capital gains already get favorable tax treatment compared with wage income. The Tax Foundation estimated that the top fifth of taxpayers would receive a boost to after tax income more than 10 times as great as the lowest fifth if gains were indexed to prices.

 

It’s unlikely to happen with so much red ink already flowing in Washington. The Yale Budget Lab calculated that indexing capital gains would cost Uncle Sam $1 trillion over a decade if applied retroactively. 

 

Even so, the conversation over inflation’s drag is worth having. The bull market of the past several years may have left savers feeling rich, but it got a boost from gains that don’t translate into nearly as much bread, gasoline or college tuition. 

 

The S&P 500’s annualized return over the past five calendar years falls from 14.3% to 9.5% when adjusted for buying power. Inflation ran above the Federal Reserve’s target for nearly that entire span. 

 

The preceding 10 years looks less impressive at first glance with a headline annualized gain of just 13.8%. But investors kept much more of it with an inflation-adjusted return of 11.8%.

 

Even before accounting for capital gains, “the cruelest tax” sneakily picks thrifty people’s pockets with no act of Congress required.
